hibbing.happened: He was born in Duluth in 1941, the elder son of Abram and Beatty Zimmerman. When he was six the family moved inland to Hibbing, a mining town on the Mesabi Iron Range, where his father worked in the family's furniture and appliance store. He grew up in a close Jewish household, formed teenage bands, and in 1959 left for the University of Minnesota. In the Dinkytown student neighborhood he spent more time in coffeehouses than in class, and there he took a new name.
hibbing.music: No records survive from these years, but the listening that shaped everything later began here. Late at night he tuned in distant radio stations playing country, blues and early rock and roll, and he idolized Little Richard, pounding the piano with his high-school bands. In Minneapolis he swapped the piano for an acoustic guitar and harmonica, learning old ballads and blues from records and from other players, and above all absorbing the songs and the plain-spoken manner of Woody Guthrie.
hibbing.ledTo: Guthrie became a fixation. Dylan learned his songs, imitated his voice and read his life story, and when he heard that his hero was seriously ill in a hospital near New York, the Midwest stopped being big enough. He left the university without finishing, played his way east, and reached New York in the winter of 1961. He arrived with a guitar, a borrowed manner and a head full of old songs, and the city's folk scene was ready for someone like him.

village.happened: He made his first visits to Woody Guthrie in a New Jersey hospital and played wherever he could in the Village, from basket houses to Gerde's Folk City. A warm review by Robert Shelton in the New York Times helped bring a contract with Columbia, signed by the producer John Hammond. Over the next two years his songs were taken up by others and by the civil-rights movement; he sang at the Newport Folk Festival with Joan Baez and at the March on Washington in 1963.
village.music: The debut album was mostly traditional blues and folk songs with just two originals, sung with young bravado. The Freewheelin' Bob Dylan, built around songs like "Blowin' in the Wind" and "A Hard Rain's a-Gonna Fall," showed a writer of startling reach. The Times They Are a-Changin' was starker and more topical. Another Side of Bob Dylan, cut in a single night in 1964, set the protest aside for personal songs, jokes and love. Throughout, it was only his voice, guitar and harmonica.
village.ledTo: By 1964 he was uncomfortable being treated as a spokesman, and his writing was moving toward longer, stranger songs built on images rather than headlines. He was also listening closely to the Beatles and the new British bands and seeing what a group could do. The next step was to plug in. His following album put a rock band behind half of its songs, and within months the acoustic folk singer of the Village was gone for good.

electric.happened: Bringing It All Back Home came out in the spring of 1965, just before a solo acoustic tour of England that D. A. Pennebaker filmed for Dont Look Back. That July at Newport he played a short, loud set backed by members of the Paul Butterfield Blues Band, and part of the crowd booed. Late in the year he married Sara Lownds. He then toured the world with the Hawks, meeting hostile audiences night after night; in Manchester in 1966 one listener shouted Judas at him.
electric.music: The sound changed faster than at any other point in his career. Bringing It All Back Home split its time between a rough electric band and solo acoustic songs. "Like a Rolling Stone," six minutes long and built on Al Kooper's organ, became a hit single, and Highway 61 Revisited, with Mike Bloomfield's guitar, carried the same wild energy across a whole album. Blonde on Blonde, a double album made mostly in Nashville, was looser and more shimmering, full of long, dreamlike songs.
electric.ledTo: The pace was impossible to keep up. The 1966 tour, with its booing crowds and punishing schedule, left him exhausted, and more concerts were planned. Then, in the summer of 1966, he crashed his motorcycle near his home in Woodstock, New York. The accident gave him a reason to stop. He cancelled the road, withdrew from public view and stayed home with his young family, and for more than a year almost nothing new was heard from him.

basement.happened: He spent his recovery out of sight in Woodstock, raising a growing family and turning down the role of rock star. In 1967 the Hawks moved nearby, and in the basement of a pink house in West Saugerties they recorded dozens of songs for fun. His only major concert of these years was at the Isle of Wight Festival in 1969, with the Band. In 1970 Princeton gave him an honorary doctorate, a ceremony he found uncomfortable and later turned into a song.
basement.music: The basement recordings were loose, funny and haunted, mixing old folk songs with new ones, and they spread on bootlegs long before any official release. John Wesley Harding, cut in Nashville with just bass and drums, was spare and parable-like. Nashville Skyline went further into country, with a smooth new voice and a duet with Johnny Cash. Self Portrait, a puzzling double album of covers and odds and ends, was widely panned, and New Morning followed within months, warmer and more confident.
basement.ledTo: The early seventies were quiet. He released little new music, moved his family back to New York for a time and seemed content to stay out of the spotlight. Gradually he edged back: a role and a soundtrack in a Sam Peckinpah western, a brief move away from Columbia, and plans to go back on the road with the Band, the same musicians who had stood beside him through the booing of 1966. A new, more open chapter was about to begin.

tracks.happened: In Mexico in 1972 and 1973 he acted in Sam Peckinpah's Pat Garrett and Billy the Kid and wrote its score. In 1974 he returned to the road with the Band for an arena tour that drew enormous demand. His marriage, meanwhile, was falling apart, and he and Sara divorced in 1977. In between came the Rolling Thunder Revue of 1975 and 1976, a roving caravan of friends playing smaller halls, and in 1978 a long tour of Japan, Australia, Europe and America.
tracks.music: The soundtrack gave him "Knockin' on Heaven's Door". Planet Waves was made quickly with the Band, and Columbia released the outtakes album Dylan without his blessing. Blood on the Tracks, recorded in New York and partly redone in Minneapolis, was intimate and mostly acoustic. The Basement Tapes finally appeared officially in 1975. Desire, much of it written with Jacques Levy, was coloured by Scarlet Rivera's violin and Emmylou Harris's harmonies. Street-Legal brought horns and a chorus of backing singers.
tracks.ledTo: By the end of the 1978 tour he had been through a divorce, a sprawling film of his own, Renaldo and Clara, that few liked, and years of nearly nonstop movement. Late that year, by his own account, he had a religious experience and became a born-again Christian, joining Bible classes in California. The songs he began writing came out of that faith, and his next album, recorded in Muscle Shoals, Alabama, would surprise almost everyone who had followed him.

gospel.happened: His conversion became public in 1979. That autumn he appeared on Saturday Night Live and played three songs from his new album, and in November he opened a run of shows at the Warfield Theatre in San Francisco that included none of his older songs, with sermons between numbers. Many listeners walked out or stayed away. In 1980 he won a Grammy for "Gotta Serve Somebody," and by the end of that year the old songs had begun to return to his concerts.
gospel.music: Slow Train Coming, produced by Jerry Wexler and Barry Beckett in Muscle Shoals with Mark Knopfler on guitar, was the best-sounding record he had made in years, tight and soulful. Saved went deeper into gospel, with a band and a chorus of backing singers in full voice. Shot of Love, in 1981, was rougher and more varied, mixing faith songs with earthier rock and roll, and it ended with "Every Grain of Sand," often counted among the finest songs he has written.
gospel.ledTo: By 1981 his shows mixed the gospel songs with old favourites, and the preaching had faded from the stage. He never publicly renounced his faith, but his songs stopped announcing it so directly. When he returned to the studio in 1983 it was with Mark Knopfler as producer, and the album that resulted, Infidels, was full of worldly, political and personal songs. The gospel period closed, leaving three records that are still argued over and, more lately, increasingly admired.

eighties.happened: These were restless years. In 1985 he closed the Live Aid concert in Philadelphia with Keith Richards and Ronnie Wood, and a passing remark about American farmers helped spark Farm Aid. He toured with Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers and then with the Grateful Dead. In 1988 Bruce Springsteen inducted him into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, he formed the Traveling Wilburys with George Harrison, Jeff Lynne, Roy Orbison and Tom Petty, and he began the long road he never really left.
eighties.music: Infidels, with Knopfler and the rhythm section of Sly Dunbar and Robbie Shakespeare, was polished and strong. After it he chased the sound of the radio: Empire Burlesque was dressed in glossy mid-eighties production, Knocked Out Loaded was patchy but included the long "Brownsville Girl," written with Sam Shepard, and Down in the Groove was mostly covers. Oh Mercy, made in New Orleans with Daniel Lanois, was dark and atmospheric and widely hailed. Under the Red Sky, produced by Don and David Was, was lighter.
eighties.ledTo: Under the Red Sky was coolly received, and after it the new songs dried up. Dylan kept touring year round with a small band, often playing over a hundred shows a year, but for most of the 1990s he released no new songs of his own. Instead he went back to the beginning, to the old folk ballads and country blues he had learned in Minneapolis and the Village, and began recording them on his own at home, just a guitar, a harmonica and his voice.

roots.happened: He kept touring, and the industry began to look back at his career. In 1992 Columbia staged a thirtieth-anniversary concert at Madison Square Garden, where Neil Young, Stevie Wonder, Eddie Vedder, George Harrison and many others played his songs before he took the stage himself. In January 1993 he sang "Chimes of Freedom" at the celebration in Washington for Bill Clinton's inauguration. Through it all he was writing very little and spending much of his time on the road.
roots.music: Good as I Been to You, recorded in his garage studio in Malibu, was a set of traditional songs and old ballads played solo on acoustic guitar and harmonica, his first album like that since 1964. World Gone Wrong, the next year, was darker and starker still, made up of murder ballads, blues and laments, and came with his own idiosyncratic notes on each song. It won a Grammy for traditional folk. The voice was worn, but the performances were intimate and unhurried.
roots.ledTo: These records sent him back to the deep well of old American song, and that well would feed everything he wrote afterward. In 1994 he played an MTV Unplugged show. Then he began writing again, and early in 1997 he went back into the studio with Daniel Lanois, carrying a new set of songs about age, love and mortality. Those songs became Time Out of Mind, released that autumn after a serious illness had put him in hospital, and the start of a remarkable late flowering.

renaissance.happened: The years after Time Out of Mind brought honours he had never sought: the Album of the Year Grammy, an Oscar and a Golden Globe for "Things Have Changed" from the film Wonder Boys, a special Pulitzer citation and, in 2012, the Presidential Medal of Freedom. Chronicles: Volume One, a vivid, unconventional memoir, appeared in 2004, and Martin Scorsese's No Direction Home followed. He hosted Theme Time Radio Hour on satellite radio, and he never stopped touring the world.
renaissance.music: Time Out of Mind, produced by Daniel Lanois, was murky and brooding, full of songs about time running out. "Love and Theft" and Modern Times were made with his road band and produced by Dylan himself, under the name Jack Frost, playing jump blues, swing, rockabilly and old ballads with relish. Together Through Life leaned on David Hidalgo's accordion and Tex-Mex textures, Christmas in the Heart gave its earnings to charity, and Tempest closed the run with long, dark story songs.
renaissance.ledTo: After Tempest the new songs paused once more. On stage his voice had grown deep and rough, yet he had become fascinated by the craft of singing itself and by the popular songs of his parents' generation. Rather than write, he began recording with his touring band the ballads that Frank Sinatra had once made famous. The result, Shadows in the Night, would open a new and quite unexpected chapter: Bob Dylan as a singer of the Great American Songbook.

standards.happened: In 2015 he was named MusiCares Person of the Year and gave a long, frank speech about his influences and his critics. In October 2016 the Swedish Academy awarded him the Nobel Prize in Literature. He stayed silent for weeks, did not attend the ceremony in Stockholm, where Patti Smith sang one of his songs in his place, and the following year delivered a recorded lecture about the songs and books that had formed him, including Moby-Dick, All Quiet on the Western Front and the Odyssey.
standards.music: Shadows in the Night, recorded at Capitol Studios in Hollywood, set Sinatra's ballads for his small touring band, with a pedal steel guitar standing in for the orchestra. It was played largely live, with few overdubs, and his voice, gentler than on stage, carried the melodies with real care. Fallen Angels followed in 2016 in the same spirit, a little lighter, and Triplicate in 2017 stretched the project across three discs, thirty songs in all, with more brass and swing.
standards.ledTo: The standards years changed how people heard him as a singer, and his concerts began to mix these old ballads with his own songs. Then came a long quiet in the studio. Few knew he was writing again until March 2020, when, with much of the world shut in by the pandemic, he released without warning a seventeen-minute song about the Kennedy assassination. It was his first new original song in eight years, and an album soon followed.

rough.happened: The surprise release of "Murder Most Foul" in March 2020 was followed in June by Rough and Rowdy Ways, which drew some of the best reviews of his career. Late that year he sold his songwriting catalog to Universal Music Publishing Group. In 2021 he streamed Shadow Kingdom, a concert film staged in a smoky, invented club, and in 2022 published The Philosophy of Modern Song. The Bob Dylan Center opened in Tulsa, and he returned to touring, playing mostly the new songs.
rough.music: Rough and Rowdy Ways is slow, patient and grave. Much of it is low-lit blues and hushed ballads, with his voice close and conversational, and the songs are crowded with references to history, literature and old music. The long Kennedy song fills a disc of its own. Shadow Kingdom took the opposite approach to the past, reimagining older songs, many from the sixties, as quiet, acoustic, almost chamber-like arrangements, and it later came out as an album of its own.
rough.ledTo: The story of this era is still being written. In his eighties he keeps touring, building sets around his newest songs rather than his most famous ones. The center in Tulsa has made his archive available to researchers, and a 2024 biopic about his arrival in New York, A Complete Unknown, brought his early years to a new generation. Whatever comes next, he has spent more than sixty years refusing to stand still, and shows no sign of stopping.

moments.born-in-duluth: Duluth is a port city at the western tip of Lake Superior, and his parents belonged to its small Jewish community; his father Abram worked for Standard Oil there. The boy spent only his first few years in the city before the family moved inland to the Iron Range, so most of what later shaped him came from Hibbing rather than the harbor town. Duluth still turns up in his story. In his Nobel lecture he recalled seeing Buddy Holly play the Duluth Armory in early 1959, just days before Holly died, and described that show as a turning point for him. Decades later the city began marking its connection to him, and the house where he spent his earliest years still stands on a hillside above the lake.
moments.move-to-hibbing: Abram Zimmerman's illness ended his job in Duluth, and in Hibbing he went into business with his brothers, running a furniture and appliance store. Hibbing was built around one of the largest open-pit iron mines in the world, a cold, working town far from any music industry. That distance mattered. Late at night the boy listened to faraway radio stations that carried country, blues and early rhythm and blues, and Hank Williams became one of his first heroes. He had a younger brother, David, and a fairly ordinary small-town childhood, including his bar mitzvah in 1954. Years later he would speak of the town with mixed feelings, but the landscape and the sense of isolation stayed with him and surface again and again in his songs about the North Country.
moments.hibbing-high-graduation: By his teens he was banging out Little Richard numbers on the piano and leading a string of short-lived school bands, among them the Golden Chords. At least one talent-show performance was loud enough that the school cut it short, a story classmates told for years afterwards. He also had a high school girlfriend, Echo Helstrom, often named as an inspiration for his later song "Girl from the North Country". Rock and roll, more than folk music, was his passion at this point, and he dreamed of the kind of stardom Elvis Presley had. Graduation meant leaving Hibbing. That summer he briefly played piano with Bobby Vee's band in Fargo, and in the autumn he moved south to Minneapolis, where his musical direction would change quickly.
moments.university-of-minnesota: Dinkytown was the bohemian neighborhood next to the campus, full of coffeehouses, bookshops and student apartments. There he traded rock and roll for acoustic folk music, learning old ballads and blues from records borrowed from friends and playing for small change at places like the Ten O'Clock Scholar. Reading Woody Guthrie's autobiography, Bound for Glory, and hearing his records changed everything: he began to dress, talk and sing in Guthrie's style. He spent little time on his studies and drifted away from the university within about a year. The new name stuck, and so did his ambition. Near the end of 1960 he decided that Minneapolis was too small, and he set out for New York, where the folk revival was at its center and where he hoped to meet Guthrie himself.
moments.arrives-in-new-york: He arrived in the middle of a hard winter and found his way to Greenwich Village, where he played for tips at the Cafe Wha? and other clubs and slept on friends' couches. Guthrie, his idol, was by then too ill to perform, living in Greystone Park Psychiatric Hospital in New Jersey. Dylan visited him there, played him songs and also called on him at the home of friends who hosted Guthrie on Sundays. Out of those visits came "Song to Woody", one of the first strong songs he wrote, a tribute that later appeared on his debut album. The encounters gave the newcomer a direct link to the folk tradition he admired, and within months he had become a familiar figure on the Village scene, learning from older singers such as Dave Van Ronk.
moments.shelton-review: Dylan was opening for the bluegrass group the Greenbriar Boys at Gerde's, but Shelton's review gave the young unknown most of the attention, praising his originality and his rough charm. Around the same time he played harmonica on a recording session for the singer Carolyn Hester, where the veteran producer John Hammond noticed him. Hammond offered him a contract with Columbia, an unusual move for a major label with a scruffy folk singer, and some at the company doubted the decision. His first album, Bob Dylan, was recorded quickly in late 1961 and came out in 1962. It consisted mostly of traditional songs and blues, with only two originals, and sold modestly. Shelton remained a supporter and later wrote a full biography of him.
moments.newport-1963: Newport was the most important gathering of the folk revival, and in 1963 Dylan arrived there as its rising star. His second album, The Freewheelin' Bob Dylan, had come out that spring, and Peter, Paul and Mary had turned "Blowin' in the Wind" into a hit. Joan Baez, already famous, brought him on stage with her and championed his songs, and the two became a public pairing. The closing scene, with the Freedom Singers, Pete Seeger, Baez and others singing together, tied his music to the civil rights movement in the public mind. Baez soon invited him on her own tour as a guest, introducing him to larger audiences. He returned to Newport in 1964 and again in 1965, when his appearance would go very differently.
moments.march-on-washington: The march drew a vast crowd to the Lincoln Memorial, and the musical program included Joan Baez, Odetta, Mahalia Jackson and Peter, Paul and Mary. Dylan's song was about the murder of the civil rights leader Medgar Evers in Mississippi earlier that summer, and it argued that the man who pulled the trigger was a tool of politicians who stirred up racial hatred. He also sang "When the Ship Comes In" with Baez. Later that afternoon Martin Luther King Jr. gave his famous speech. The day sealed his image as a voice of the movement, an image he soon found confining. Within a year he was writing more personal songs, and Another Side of Bob Dylan, released in 1964, moved away from topical protest.
moments.dont-look-back-tour-1965: The tour came just after Bringing It All Back Home, an album with one electric side and one acoustic side, yet on stage he still appeared alone with guitar and harmonica. British fans treated him as a star, and the press followed him everywhere. Pennebaker's camera caught the backstage life: sparring with reporters, hotel-room song swaps, Joan Baez in the entourage, a meeting with Donovan, and his manager Albert Grossman at work. The film's opening, with Dylan flipping cue cards to "Subterranean Homesick Blues", became one of the most imitated images in music. It was the last tour of his solo acoustic period. Weeks after returning home he recorded "Like a Rolling Stone", and the sound of his music changed for good.
moments.newport-1965: Newport had celebrated him as a folk hero, so the change was startling. With Mike Bloomfield on guitar, Al Kooper on organ and a rhythm section from the Butterfield band, he played only three songs, including "Maggie's Farm" and the newly released "Like a Rolling Stone". Some of the crowd jeered; how many, and whether at the music, the poor sound or the short set, has been argued about ever since. He came back alone with an acoustic guitar for two more songs. The night became the best-known symbol of folk music meeting rock. Highway 61 Revisited followed within weeks, and he soon went on tour with the Hawks, facing similar hostility. The 2024 film A Complete Unknown ends with this night.
moments.marries-sara-lownds: Sara had a young daughter, Maria, from her first marriage, whom Dylan later adopted. The wedding was kept so quiet that the press did not learn of it for months. The couple had four more children together, including Jesse, born in early 1966, and Jakob, who later led the band the Wallflowers. After the frenzy of 1965 and 1966 they settled into family life in Woodstock, and he largely kept his private life out of view. Many listeners connect "Sad Eyed Lady of the Lowlands", the long closing song of Blonde on Blonde, with her, and he later wrote "Sara" for Desire. The marriage ran into trouble in the mid 1970s, and they divorced in 1977.
moments.motorcycle-accident: The crash came at the end of an exhausting stretch of recording and touring, with more concerts already booked. How badly he was hurt has never been fully clear; no detailed medical account was made public, and he recovered privately, partly at the home of a doctor in Middletown, New York. Whatever the injuries, the accident gave him a reason to stop. He cancelled his upcoming shows, spent time with his growing family and stayed out of public view. In that quiet he made the basement recordings with the Hawks and then John Wesley Harding, a spare, restrained record very unlike his mid-1960s sound. Apart from a handful of one-off appearances, he did not tour again until 1974, and the accident has fed his legend ever since.
moments.judas-manchester-1966: On that 1966 tour each concert had two halves: a quiet acoustic set, then a loud one with the Hawks, and many folk fans booed the second half night after night. In Manchester a voice from the audience called him a traitor in the harshest terms. Dylan answered that he did not believe him and called him a liar, then turned to the band and told them to play loud before launching into "Like a Rolling Stone". The recording circulated for decades on bootlegs mislabeled as the Royal Albert Hall concert. Columbia officially released it in 1998 as Live 1966, part of the Bootleg Series, and it is now regarded as one of the great live rock recordings. More than one man has since claimed to be the heckler.
moments.basement-sessions: The sessions were relaxed and unplanned. Garth Hudson ran a tape recorder while the group worked through old folk ballads, country songs and blues alongside a stream of new Dylan songs, some funny, some strange, some deeply serious, among them "I Shall Be Released" and "This Wheel's on Fire". Demo tapes went to his music publisher, and other artists such as Manfred Mann and the Byrds had hits with the songs. A bootleg called Great White Wonder appeared in 1969, one of the first rock bootlegs. Columbia issued a selection as The Basement Tapes in 1975 and a near-complete set in 2014. The Band's own debut, Music from Big Pink, came out in 1968, and the sessions helped shape the rootsier sound of the late 1960s.
moments.isle-of-wight-1969: He had turned down the chance to play Woodstock, near his own home, a few weeks earlier, so the British show carried huge expectations. A very large crowd came, and members of the Beatles were among those who watched. He performed for about an hour, dressed in a white suit, singing in the softer, smoother voice of his recent Nashville Skyline and reworking older songs in country style. Some critics and fans who had waited years were disappointed by the short, mellow set; others found it warm and relaxed. A few of the performances appeared on Self Portrait in 1970, and the full concert was released decades later as part of the Bootleg Series. It was his last major concert before the Band tour of 1974.
moments.princeton-doctorate: He went to the ceremony reluctantly, accompanied by his wife Sara and David Crosby, and found the formality uncomfortable. It was a hot day, and the air was full of the noise of cicadas emerging that summer. He wrote about the experience as "Day of the Locusts", released on New Morning later in 1970, and recalled it again in his memoir Chronicles, Volume One. The degree was an early sign that the academic world took him seriously as a writer, at a time when his new records were getting mixed reviews. Far larger honors came later: a special Pulitzer citation in 2008, the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2012 and the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2016.
moments.pat-garrett-film-1973: The film starred James Coburn as Pat Garrett and Kris Kristofferson as Billy the Kid, and was shot in Durango, Mexico, in a production troubled by clashes between Peckinpah and the studio. Dylan's part was small and enigmatic, a drifter who attaches himself to Billy's gang. His music did more. The soundtrack album, released in 1973, is mostly instrumental, but it includes "Knockin' on Heaven's Door", which became a hit and one of his most covered songs, later recorded by Eric Clapton and Guns N' Roses among many others. MGM released a cut version of the film that Peckinpah disowned, and fuller versions appeared later. Soon after, Dylan left Columbia for a time and signed with Asylum Records.
moments.tour-1974: The tour was promoted by Bill Graham, and demand for tickets was enormous, with millions of mail-order requests for the available seats. It followed the release of Planet Waves, recorded with the Band and issued on Asylum, his first studio album with them. On stage the music was loud and urgent, with Dylan pushing his older songs hard and the Band playing sets of their own between his. Before the Flood, drawn largely from the final shows in Los Angeles, came out later in 1974. The tour proved he could still fill arenas after eight years away. Before the year was out he had returned to Columbia and recorded Blood on the Tracks, often counted among his finest albums.
moments.rolling-thunder-revue-1975: The revue was loose and theatrical. Alongside Baez and McGuinn came Bob Neuwirth, Ramblin' Jack Elliott, Mick Ronson, violinist Scarlet Rivera and the poet Allen Ginsberg, with Joni Mitchell joining partway. Dylan often performed in white face paint, and the shows mixed old songs with new ones from Desire, which came out in early 1976. The playwright Sam Shepard traveled along to help with a film, which became Renaldo and Clara, released in 1978. The first leg ended with a benefit for the imprisoned boxer Rubin Carter at Madison Square Garden. A second leg in 1976 produced the album Hard Rain and a television special, and in 2019 Martin Scorsese made a playful documentary about the tour.
moments.world-tour-1978: The tour began in Japan early in the year and ran for most of the next ten months, ending in the United States in December. Dylan reworked his old songs with a big band that included saxophone and a trio of women singers, giving many of them new arrangements, sometimes almost unrecognizable. In the middle of the year he released Street-Legal. European audiences responded warmly, including a very large outdoor show at Blackbushe in England, while some American critics mocked the glossy sound as showbusiness. At Budokan, recorded in Tokyo, was issued first in Japan and then worldwide. Near the end of the tour he went through a religious conversion, and by early 1979 he had become a born-again Christian.
moments.snl-1979: He played "Gotta Serve Somebody", "I Believe in You" and "When You Gonna Wake Up", all from Slow Train Coming, the album he had made in Muscle Shoals, Alabama, with producers Jerry Wexler and Barry Beckett and Mark Knopfler on guitar. Backed by a tight band and gospel singers, he left no doubt that his new Christian faith was the subject of his music now. For a television audience used to the older Dylan, it was a striking statement. About two weeks later he began a run of shows in San Francisco where he played only his new religious songs, to some boos and walkouts. "Gotta Serve Somebody" went on to win him a Grammy, and the gospel period continued with Saved in 1980.
moments.warfield-gospel-shows-1979: The run came a few months after Slow Train Coming, the album that announced his conversion to evangelical Christianity. Fans who bought tickets expecting the familiar songs heard none of them. Instead he fronted a band with a group of gospel backing singers and performed the new religious material, along with songs that would turn up on his next album, Saved, and on some nights he spoke to the crowd about his faith between numbers. Some in the audience booed or walked out, and several reviews were openly hostile. He did not bend. The gospel-only format carried on through the touring that followed into 1980, and for a while it was the only version of Dylan on offer. Whatever people made of the message, the shows held some of the most fervent singing of his career.
moments.grammy-1980: The award went to the lead single from Slow Train Coming, the first record of his gospel period. It was a striking piece of mainstream approval at a moment when many longtime listeners were confused or put off by his new direction. At the ceremony he performed the song with his touring band and backing singers, carrying its religious message to a national television audience. The song had also provoked John Lennon, who recorded a mocking home demo in reply. The win suggested the gospel records could still reach a broad public, even as the next album, Saved, met a cooler reception later that year. It remains one of the clearest signs of how seriously the music business took this chapter while it was happening, whatever critics would later decide about it.
moments.musical-retrospective-1980: A year after the gospel-only concerts, he came back to the same San Francisco theater with a different idea of what a show could hold. The religious songs were still there, but now they shared the stage with older material, some of it rearranged, and with new songs pointing toward his next record. Guests sat in on several nights; one was Mike Bloomfield, the guitarist from his 1965 electric sessions, who joined him for a couple of songs only months before his own death. The change showed that the strictest phase of his gospel years was easing. The album that followed in 1981, Shot of Love, mixed faith with other subjects, and from then on his concerts drew freely on every part of his catalog again.
moments.live-aid-1985: Live Aid was a two-continent benefit for famine relief in Ethiopia, broadcast around the world from London and Philadelphia. Dylan was placed near the end of the American show, playing acoustic guitar with Richards and Wood beside him. The set was rough: the three could barely hear themselves while preparations for the finale went on behind the curtain, and guitar strings gave trouble. Many viewers remembered it as a ragged moment on a huge stage. Yet one passing remark mattered more than the music. He suggested from the stage that some of the money might help American farmers losing their land to debt. Willie Nelson, Neil Young and John Mellencamp took up the idea, and the first Farm Aid concert was held that September, an event that has continued ever since.
moments.hall-of-fame-1988: He entered the Hall in only its third year of inductions, in a class that also included the Beatles, the Beach Boys, the Drifters and the Supremes. Springsteen's speech became one of the best remembered in the institution's history. He described first hearing Dylan on the radio as a teenager and how it changed his sense of what a rock record could say, and he credited Dylan with freeing the minds of a generation of songwriters. Dylan's own remarks were brief and wry. The honor arrived at an odd point in his career, after a run of records that had drawn mixed reviews. Within months he would start the touring that defined his later decades and join the Traveling Wilburys, and the following year Oh Mercy would restore much of his critical standing.
moments.never-ending-tour-begins: After big stadium tours with Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers and with the Grateful Dead, he cut his live show down to a small, hard-hitting band led by guitarist G.E. Smith and started playing far more often. The idea was to treat performing as steady work rather than as a special event, and to keep the songs alive by changing them night after night. The name came from an interview the following year, and Dylan himself never much liked it, but it stuck. For years he played around a hundred shows annually or more, reshaping arrangements, swapping musicians, and moving through theaters, arenas, festivals and minor-league ballparks. The road became the center of his working life, and for many listeners the concerts, more than any album, became the place to hear where he was going next.
moments.traveling-wilburys-1988: The group began almost by accident. Harrison needed an extra track for a single and gathered friends to record it, using a studio at Dylan's home in Malibu. The result, "Handle with Care", was too good to tuck away, so the five agreed to make a whole album together under joking pseudonyms as brothers of a fictional Wilbury family. The record, recorded quickly and loosely, had the warm, easy sound of friends trading verses, with each member taking turns at lead vocals. It became a big hit and won a Grammy. Orbison died that December, only weeks after its release. The remaining four made a second album in 1990, wryly titled Vol. 3, and the project gave Dylan a rare taste of being one voice in a band.
moments.bobfest-1992: Neil Young nicknamed the night Bobfest, and the name stuck. The bill was enormous: Stevie Wonder, Lou Reed, Johnny Cash, Eric Clapton, George Harrison, Tom Petty, Roger McGuinn and Young himself were among those who sang his songs, with Booker T. and the MG's as the house band. The evening is also remembered for Sinéad O'Connor, who was booed so loudly, weeks after a televised protest against the pope, that she abandoned her planned song. Dylan came out at the end, played alone for a few songs, then led an all-star group through a couple of his classics. The concert was released as an album and video the following year. Its broad roster showed how deeply his songs had spread through every corner of popular music over three decades.
moments.clinton-inaugural-1993: The concert at the Lincoln Memorial was a public celebration held in the days before Clinton took office, with a long list of performers. Dylan chose "Chimes of Freedom", a song from 1964, rather than one of his better known anthems. Clinton was the first president to come of age in the rock era, and the song's vision of freedom fit the evening's theme of a new generation taking charge. For Dylan, who had spent decades refusing the role of spokesman for anything, it was a rare appearance at an official political occasion. It also showed how far his early songs had moved from protest folk to national heritage. He returned to the White House years later, performing at a 2010 concert honoring the music of the civil rights movement.
moments.grammy-album-of-the-year-1998: Time Out of Mind, made with producer Daniel Lanois, had come out the previous autumn to the strongest reviews he had received in decades. Its release followed closely on a serious illness in 1997, a heart infection that put him in hospital, and the album's dark, weary atmosphere was widely read in that light. Besides Album of the Year it took Best Contemporary Folk Album, and "Cold Irons Bound" won a rock vocal award. The ceremony is also remembered for a stranger moment: during his performance of "Love Sick", a man with words scrawled on his bare chest jumped beside him and danced until he was led away, while Dylan kept playing. The awards confirmed a late-career revival that his next records would build on.
moments.oscar-things-have-changed: Curtis Hanson's film Wonder Boys starred Michael Douglas as a stalled novelist and teacher, and Dylan wrote the song to suit its rueful, worn-out mood. The track pairs a loping groove with a narrator who sounds detached and slightly amused by his own decline, close in spirit to the voice of Time Out of Mind. When the Oscar was awarded in 2001 he was on tour in Australia, so he performed the song by satellite link from there. Afterward he kept the statuette with him on the road and often placed it on an amplifier or the stage, a small joke repeated night after night. The award brought his writing to a wide new audience and set the stage for the album that followed later that year, Love and Theft.
moments.chronicles-volume-one: Instead of a straight life story, the book jumps between a few chosen periods. It spends long stretches on his arrival in New York in the early 1960s, on the folk scene, the clubs and the people who taught him; then turns to a family-centered stretch around 1970 when he tried to escape the role others assigned him; and to the making of Oh Mercy in New Orleans with Daniel Lanois at the end of the 1980s. The writing is vivid, funny and often unexpected, full of portraits of musicians and books that shaped him. Readers who had expected evasions found a generous, detailed storyteller. It was billed as the first of several volumes, but no second volume has followed, and his next major book came nearly two decades later.
moments.presidential-medal-of-freedom: The Medal of Freedom is the highest civilian honor in the United States. Dylan received it in the same ceremony as a varied group of others, among them the novelist Toni Morrison, the astronaut and senator John Glenn, and former Secretary of State Madeleine Albright. Obama spoke of being a fan and of what Dylan's music had meant to him as a young man, and Dylan, wearing dark glasses, accepted the medal quietly. The honor followed other official recognitions, including a special Pulitzer Prize citation in 2008, and came two years after he had played at the White House in a concert celebrating the music of the civil rights movement. It placed his songs firmly among American cultural achievements several years before the Nobel committee did the same on an international stage.
moments.musicares-2015: MusiCares, the charity linked to the Grammys that helps musicians in need, chose him as its honoree, and a lineup of artists performed his songs at a benefit dinner. Then he took the stage with a prepared text and spoke for around half an hour, an extraordinary length for a man known for terse public remarks. He traced his songs back to the folk, blues and country music he had absorbed when young, explaining how old forms had fed his writing. He thanked the people who had helped him early on, and he also hit back at critics who had complained about his voice for decades, and at a few fellow musicians he felt had slighted him. The speech was widely published afterward and remains one of the clearest accounts he has given of how he works.
moments.nobel-prize-2016: The announcement in October set off a debate about whether songs belonged in a literary prize, and Dylan made it stranger by staying silent for about two weeks; one academy member publicly called that silence rude. He eventually said he was honored but did not travel to the December ceremony in Stockholm, citing other commitments. Patti Smith sang "A Hard Rain's A-Gonna Fall" in his place, pausing emotionally partway through, and a short speech he had written was read at the banquet. He accepted the medal and diploma privately in Stockholm the following spring, while on tour. To collect the prize money he still had to deliver a lecture, which he did that June. The award placed him in a line of writers stretching back over a century.
moments.nobel-lecture-2017: The academy's rules required a lecture within six months of the December ceremony, and he sent his as an audio recording, read over a quiet piano. He began with the music that first stirred him, recalling seeing Buddy Holly perform shortly before Holly's death and discovering Lead Belly and the folk tradition. Then he turned to three books from his school years that had stayed with him: Moby-Dick, All Quiet on the Western Front and The Odyssey, retelling each in his own way. He ended by arguing that songs are meant to be sung and heard, not just read on a page. Some writers later pointed to close similarities between parts of his Moby-Dick passage and an online study guide, adding one more twist to an already unusual laureateship.
moments.murder-most-foul-release: He posted the song at midnight with a short note thanking fans and wishing them safety, and it arrived as many people were first sheltering at home. Built on soft piano, violin and light percussion, it unfolds slowly over seventeen minutes, its spoken-sung verses moving from the shooting in Dallas into a long roll call of songs, films and performers from American culture. Nothing like it had come from him in years, and it drew enormous attention and praise. Two more new songs followed in the next weeks, and in June he released Rough and Rowdy Ways, his first album of original songs since Tempest in 2012. The long track filled a disc of its own as the album's closer, and the record was greeted as one of his strongest late works.
moments.catalog-sale-2020: The deal covered his rights in more than six hundred songs, written across six decades, from his earliest records to his newest. No official price was announced, though it was widely reported to be in the hundreds of millions of dollars. The sale was among the largest of a wave of catalog deals in those years, as investors and publishers paid record sums for the songwriting rights of veteran artists, and it drew attention partly because Dylan had long been seen as fiercely protective of his work. Universal gained control of licensing the songs for films, advertisements and cover versions. About a year later he made a separate agreement selling the rights to his recorded music to Sony, which had long released his albums through Columbia.
moments.shadow-kingdom-2021: With live concerts halted by the pandemic, he made a film instead of a tour. Directed by Alma Har'el and shot in black and white, it placed him in a smoky, imagined nightclub, with a small band of masked musicians and an audience of extras who drank and smoked at tables. Most of the songs came from the 1960s and 1970s, slowed down, rearranged and sung in the rough, close voice of his later years, so that familiar material sounded freshly made. The event was sold as a paid online stream and surprised viewers who had expected an ordinary concert film. Later it emerged that the music on the soundtrack had been played by different musicians than those on screen. A soundtrack album appeared in 2023, and by late 2021 he was back on the road.
moments.philosophy-of-modern-song: The book collects short pieces on songs recorded by other people, ranging across early country and blues, rock and roll, pop standards and punk. Each essay usually takes two forms at once: a loose, second-person riff that imagines its way inside the song, followed by a more direct reflection on the record, the performer or the world around it. The pages are packed with photographs and pictures drawn from popular culture. Critics found it erratic, funny, opinionated and often brilliant, a portrait of his tastes as much as of the songs themselves. Its release had one embarrassment: buyers of expensive signed copies discovered the signatures had been made by machine, and the publisher and Dylan apologized and offered refunds.

albums.bob-dylan: Dylan was twenty when he walked into Columbia's New York studio in late 1961, a newcomer signed by John Hammond after a few months on the Greenwich Village club circuit. The sessions were quick and cheap: just Dylan, his acoustic guitar and his harmonica, with almost no retakes. The songs came mostly from the blues and folk repertoire he had been playing nightly, and he leans hard on death and hard luck, singing in a rasping, deliberately aged voice far older than his years. Only "Talkin' New York" and "Song to Woody", his tribute to Woody Guthrie, were his own. When the album came out in 1962 it made little impression, and some at Columbia took to calling him Hammond's folly. Yet it is a vivid snapshot of a young performer still finding himself, and within months he was writing songs that would make covers unnecessary.
albums.freewheelin: Dylan recorded his second album over many sessions between the spring of 1962 and the spring of 1963, first with John Hammond and then with Tom Wilson producing, and the running order changed more than once before release. Most of it is just Dylan alone with guitar and harmonica, though "Corrina, Corrina" carries a small backing band. The songs move freely between moods: furious protest, long visionary ballads, wry talking blues and gentle, rueful love songs shaped by his relationship with Suze Rotolo, who was away in Italy for much of the time. A song mocking the John Birch Society was dropped before release, reportedly over the label's legal worries. When Peter, Paul and Mary turned "Blowin' in the Wind" into a hit in 1963, Dylan's name spread far beyond the Village, and the album became a touchstone for the folk revival and for countless songwriters who followed.
albums.times-they-are-a-changin: Recorded in New York in the late summer and autumn of 1963 with Tom Wilson producing, his third album is the most austere record he ever made: one voice, one guitar, a harmonica, and nothing to soften the subject matter. These are songs of the civil rights era and of hard times in small towns, several drawn from real events, including the killing of Medgar Evers and the death of Hattie Carroll in Baltimore. Alongside them sit a few personal songs about distance and parting that hint at a different writer underneath. The title track was written to be an anthem and was taken up as one almost immediately. The record arrived in early 1964, just weeks after the assassination of John F. Kennedy, and it cemented his place as the voice of protest. That was a role he was already growing restless in, and within months he would set it aside.
albums.another-side: Dylan cut this album in New York in one long evening in June 1964, with Tom Wilson producing and friends drifting in and out of the studio. He played it almost entirely alone on guitar and harmonica, with piano on one track, and the loose, sometimes giggling performances reflect the speed of the session. Many of the songs had been written on travels earlier that year, including a stay in Europe. Gone were the newspaper-headline ballads; in their place came comic shaggy-dog stories, flirtatious love songs, a bitter account of a breakup and a few searching reflections on his own earlier certainties. Folk purists were dismayed, and parts of the folk press publicly scolded him for turning inward. Other artists heard something new, and the Byrds and the Turtles would soon find hits in its songs. Looking back, it is the hinge between the protest singer and the electric poet who arrived next.
albums.bringing-it-all-back-home: Recorded in New York in January 1965 with Tom Wilson producing, this album took only a few sessions, with Dylan often teaching the band songs on the spot. One side features electric guitars, bass and drums, with guitarist Bruce Langhorne among the players; the other is mostly Dylan with acoustic guitar, joined by Langhorne's shimmering electric lines on "Mr. Tambourine Man". The electric songs are fast, funny and sly, drawing on Chuck Berry and the blues, while the acoustic side holds some of his longest and darkest visions of society and self. It was released in March 1965, and that summer the Byrds took "Mr. Tambourine Man" to the top of the charts, helping launch folk rock as a genre. The album drew a clear line under his protest years and set the stage for his electric set at Newport a few months later.
albums.highway-61-revisited: The album began in June 1965 with "Like a Rolling Stone", produced by Tom Wilson; Bob Johnston took over for the rest of the summer sessions in New York. Mike Bloomfield's stinging blues guitar and Al Kooper's organ, which he improvised on a song he barely knew, define much of the sound, a rough, ringing mix of Chicago blues and rock and roll. Between the sessions came the Newport Folk Festival, where Dylan's electric set split his audience. The record is named after the highway that runs from his home state of Minnesota down through the Mississippi Delta, and it is full of grotesque characters, absurd scenes and biting humor. It closes with a long, mostly acoustic song, its guitar part played by Charlie McCoy. Released at the end of August 1965, it was hailed as a landmark, and many still rank it as his greatest album.
albums.blonde-on-blonde: Sessions began in New York with members of the Hawks, the group later known as the Band, but progress was slow. Early in 1966 producer Bob Johnston moved the work to Nashville, where seasoned players such as Charlie McCoy, Kenny Buttrey and Hargus Robbins joined Al Kooper and Robbie Robertson. The Nashville musicians often waited for hours while Dylan finished writing, then caught songs in a few takes, giving the record its relaxed, late-night glow. The sound is thinner and more delicate than the album before, built on organ, piano and lightly chiming guitars, and the songs range from brass-band larks to tender ballads and long, dreamy meditations, one of them filling an entire side. Released in mid-1966, it was quickly recognized as a high point of the decade. Weeks later his motorcycle accident ended the frantic electric period it crowned.
albums.john-wesley-harding: After the motorcycle accident in 1966 Dylan withdrew to Woodstock, and for more than a year the public heard nothing new. In late 1967 he went to Nashville with Bob Johnston and recorded this album over a few short sessions, backed only by Charlie McCoy on bass and Kenny Buttrey on drums, with Pete Drake's pedal steel added to the two closing songs. Compared with the swirling sound of 1966, it is startlingly bare: acoustic guitar, harmonica, a light rhythm section and short, carefully weighed verses. The songs read like parables, populated by outlaws, immigrants, saints and messengers, and they echo the Bible and American folklore he was steeped in at the time. Released just after Christmas 1967, at the height of psychedelia, it seemed to point rock music back toward simplicity. Jimi Hendrix's electrifying version of "All Along the Watchtower" the following year became the definitive one, as Dylan himself later acknowledged.
albums.nashville-skyline: Dylan returned to Nashville in early 1969 with Bob Johnston and many of the same session players, and the record was finished quickly. It is short, under half an hour, and it opens with a duet with Johnny Cash on a song from his second album, the result of sessions the two men shared during the visit. Most striking was his voice: smooth, warm and low, so unlike his earlier rasp that some listeners hardly knew it was him. The songs are simple, sunny country tunes about love and longing, with pedal steel and an easygoing pace, plus a bouncy instrumental. "Lay Lady Lay" became a hit single, and Dylan appeared on Cash's new television show that year. Some critics found the album slight, but it gave country music a new credibility among rock fans, and it helped open the road toward the country rock of the years that followed.
albums.new-morning: Recorded in New York in 1970, with Bob Johnston credited as producer and Al Kooper closely involved, the album followed Self Portrait by only four months. Dylan plays piano on much of it, and the sound is warm and homespun, touched with gospel, country and even a dash of jazz on one track. A few songs began as music for a stage play by the poet Archibald MacLeish, a collaboration that fell apart. Another was inspired by his trip to Princeton to receive an honorary degree that year. Elsewhere he sings about contentment, the countryside and family life, the mood of a man settled with his wife and children. Critics who had been baffled by Self Portrait greeted it with relief, some hailing it as a comeback. George Harrison soon recorded "If Not for You", and the album has kept a quiet, affectionate following ever since.
albums.self-portrait: Self Portrait was assembled from sessions in Nashville and New York in 1969 and 1970, produced by Bob Johnston, along with a handful of performances from the Isle of Wight Festival in 1969, where Dylan played with the Band. It is a sprawling double album of folk standards, pop and country covers, a few instrumentals and only a handful of originals. He sings songs by Paul Simon and Gordon Lightfoot, old ballads and pop standards, often in his Nashville croon, and some tracks carry orchestral strings and backing singers added later. Many critics took it as careless or even a deliberate joke, and Greil Marcus's long review in Rolling Stone became famous for its scorn. Dylan later suggested he had partly wanted to shake off his image as a generational prophet. In 2013 the Bootleg Series released the sessions in plainer, unadorned form as Another Self Portrait, and many listeners heard the music with fresh ears.
albums.dylan-1973: In 1973 Dylan's Columbia contract ran out and he signed with David Geffen's Asylum label. Columbia responded by putting together this album from leftover studio performances, mainly from the Self Portrait and New Morning sessions of 1969 and 1970, and releasing it late that year without his involvement. It is made entirely of covers: an Elvis Presley ballad, songs by Joni Mitchell and Jerry Jeff Walker, Peter La Farge's ballad about Ira Hayes, and several traditional folk songs. The performances lean on his Nashville-era croon and on backing singers, and many sound like warm-ups never meant for release. Critics widely regarded it as a low point and as a label's revenge on a departing star. Dylan returned to Columbia in 1974, and the album was long left out of print in many markets. Its tracks were eventually reissued as part of a large collection of his complete albums.
albums.pat-garrett: Dylan came to Sam Peckinpah's western through the screenwriter Rudy Wurlitzer, and he ended up not only writing the score but acting in the film, as a quiet drifter named Alias who rides with Billy the Kid. The music was recorded in Mexico City, where the film was shot, and later in California, with musicians including Roger McGuinn, Jim Keltner and Booker T. Jones. Much of the album is instrumental: loose guitar figures, mournful harmonica and themes that repeat in different shades, made to sit beneath the action. The film was cut by its studio against Peckinpah's wishes, and the soundtrack drew mixed reviews at the time. But one short song, "Knockin' on Heaven's Door", written for a death scene, became a hit and went on to be recorded by Eric Clapton, Guns N' Roses and many more. It ranks among the most covered songs he has ever written.
albums.planet-waves: Dylan had not made a full album of new songs in more than three years when he went into a Los Angeles studio in November 1973 with the Band, his old companions from 1966 and the basement sessions. The record was made fast, in a few days, with engineer Rob Fraboni, and the Band's playing is loose, rootsy and warm, built on Garth Hudson's organ and Robbie Robertson's guitar. The songs are mostly about home, love and devotion, with a few darker ones running underneath, and "Forever Young" appears in two contrasting versions, slow and fast. Dylan drew the cover art himself. Released in January 1974 on Asylum, it coincided with his first major tour in eight years, with the Band, which drew enormous demand for tickets. Critics were respectful rather than overwhelmed, and the album has tended to be overshadowed by the one that followed.
albums.blood-on-the-tracks: By 1974 Dylan's marriage was in trouble, and the songs he wrote that year are full of loss, anger, tenderness and memory, told with shifting points of view and time that slides back and forth. He recorded them in New York in September with a small group, the arrangements often reduced to his guitar, harmonica and a bass. Just before release, his brother David persuaded him to try some songs again in Minneapolis, where local musicians cut new versions of five of them over the holidays. Those fuller, livelier takes replaced the New York ones, giving the album its mix of intimacy and drive. It came out in January 1975 on Columbia, to which he had returned, and it was soon hailed as a masterpiece and a return to form. Dylan has played down its autobiographical side, but it remains one of the most admired breakup albums ever made.
albums.the-basement-tapes: In 1967, while Dylan recovered from his accident near Woodstock, he and the Hawks gathered almost daily to play, first at his home and then in the basement of a pink house in West Saugerties that the group shared. Garth Hudson recorded the sessions on a simple tape machine. They ran through old folk songs, country tunes and dozens of new Dylan songs, some funny and nonsensical, others haunting. Demo tapes went out to other artists, and hits followed for Manfred Mann, the Byrds and others, while bootlegs spread the music from 1969 on. When Columbia finally issued this double album in 1975, Robbie Robertson compiled it, adding tracks by the Band alone and some later overdubs. Critics welcomed it warmly, and its sound, rough, homemade and rooted in old American music, has influenced generations of musicians. The complete sessions appeared in the Bootleg Series in 2014.
albums.desire: Dylan wrote most of these songs in 1975 with the theatre director Jacques Levy, and the partnership pushed him toward long, cinematic stories. They were recorded in New York that summer with producer Don DeVito, after some crowded early sessions gave way to a lean group: Scarlet Rivera's violin, Rob Stoner's bass, Howie Wyeth's drums and Emmylou Harris singing harmony. The violin gives the album its sound, swirling and slightly exotic, with touches of Mexican and Middle Eastern color. "Hurricane" took up the case of the imprisoned boxer Rubin Carter, while "Joey" romanticized a murdered New York gangster and drew sharp criticism. The album closes with a direct, unguarded song addressed to his wife, Sara. Released in January 1976, it was a big commercial success, and many of its songs were already familiar to audiences of the Rolling Thunder Revue, the touring troupe he had launched that autumn.
albums.street-legal: After a world tour in early 1978 with a large band, Dylan took the same group into Rundown, his rehearsal studio in Santa Monica, and recorded the album in about a week with producer Don DeVito. The sound is big and soulful: saxophone, keyboards and a trio of gospel-trained women singers answering his vocals, a long way from the folk or country records of the past. The songs are dense and full of symbolic imagery, about broken relationships, spiritual searching and a sense of danger, and they foreshadow the religious turn that came soon after. The original mix was widely criticized as murky, and American critics were generally cool. In Britain it found a warmer welcome, helped by a big European tour that year. A remixed version issued in 1999 brought out the detail, and the album's reputation has risen steadily since.
albums.slow-train-coming: Late in 1978 Dylan became a born-again Christian, and the songs he wrote in the following months were about faith, sin and judgment. To record them he turned to Jerry Wexler, the veteran producer of Aretha Franklin, who brought him to Muscle Shoals in Alabama in the spring of 1979 with Barry Beckett as co-producer. The band included Mark Knopfler and drummer Pick Withers of Dire Straits, along with the Muscle Shoals horns and backing singers. The result is the most polished-sounding record he had made: tight grooves, clean guitar and a confident, often fierce vocal. Released that August, it sold well, and "Gotta Serve Somebody" brought Dylan his first Grammy for a solo vocal performance. Critics and fans were split, some admiring the music and others put off by its preaching, but it opened his most controversial chapter in earnest.
albums.saved: Dylan returned to Muscle Shoals with Jerry Wexler and Barry Beckett in February 1980, this time with the band he had been touring with since late 1979: guitarist Fred Tackett, bassist Tim Drummond, drummer Jim Keltner, keyboard players Spooner Oldham and Terry Young, and a group of gospel singers. Those shows were made up only of his new religious songs, and the album tries to bottle their energy, though it was cut quickly and some felt it lacked the spark of the stage. It sounds rawer and more churchlike than its predecessor, with call-and-response vocals, rolling piano and organ. It opens with a country gospel song, the album's one cover. Released that summer with a painting of a reaching hand on the cover, later replaced, it sold poorly and drew lukewarm reviews. Many listeners have since rediscovered these songs through live recordings from the tours.
albums.shot-of-love: Dylan recorded Shot of Love in Los Angeles in 1981, mostly with producer Chuck Plotkin, keeping the gospel singers and road musicians who had backed him on his recent tours. The sound is rougher and more rock-driven than the two records before it, with loud drums, ringing guitars and a choir of women's voices answering his lead. Alongside songs of belief sit things he had not done in two years: a tender tribute in "Lenny Bruce" to the comedian, and love songs such as "Heart of Mine". The closer, "Every Grain of Sand", is a quiet, searching hymn that many now count among his finest songs. At the time, though, reviews were cool and sales were weak, and some strong songs from the sessions were left off. Its reputation has grown since, and listeners now hear it as a bridge out of the gospel years.
albums.infidels: After three religious albums, Dylan went to the Power Station in New York in 1983 with Mark Knopfler of Dire Straits as co-producer. The band was a strong one: Sly Dunbar and Robbie Shakespeare on drums and bass, Mick Taylor and Knopfler on guitars. The result is clean and spacious, with a gentle reggae lilt under several songs and sharp guitar lines throughout. The writing ranges widely, from the shifting, dreamlike "Jokerman" to the blunt politics of "Union Sundown" and "Neighborhood Bully" and the plea of "Don't Fall Apart on Me Tonight". Knopfler left to tour before the mixing was done, and Dylan finished the record himself, reworking vocals and cutting songs. Reviewers welcomed it as a return, but fans later learned what had been dropped, above all "Blind Willie McTell", which surfaced years afterward on The Bootleg Series and is now widely seen as one of his greatest songs.
albums.empire-burlesque: Empire Burlesque was pieced together over many months of 1984 and 1985 in New York and Los Angeles, with a long and shifting list of players, including members of Tom Petty's Heartbreakers and the rhythm section of Sly Dunbar and Robbie Shakespeare. Dylan then handed the tapes to Arthur Baker, a producer known for dance remixes, who gave the mix its glossy, punchy finish. The record leans hard into the sound of mid-1980s radio, with gated drums, synthesizers, horn stabs and female backing vocals, and songs such as "Tight Connection to My Heart" were promoted with music videos. Under the sheen are romantic, sometimes witty songs that borrow freely from old films. The final track, "Dark Eyes", drops all of that for one voice, a guitar and a harmonica. Critics were divided at the time; some praised its energy, while others found the production dated it quickly. Its strongest songs have aged better than its sound.
albums.knocked-out-loaded: Knocked Out Loaded came together in 1986 around Dylan's touring with Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers, assembled from sessions old and new rather than planned as a whole. It mixes covers, gospel and country songs with co-writes: one with Petty, another with Carole Bayer Sager, and a Kris Kristofferson song sung with a children's choir. The sound swings from loose rhythm and blues to slick backing vocals, and much of it feels unfinished. At its center, though, is "Brownsville Girl", an eleven-minute song written with the playwright Sam Shepard. It began life as a different song in the Empire Burlesque sessions, and it unfolds like a road movie, drifting between a Western film, memory and a love affair, with Dylan half speaking and half singing over a full band and gospel singers. Reviews of the album were poor and sales were low, but that one song has kept a devoted following and is often named among his best.
albums.down-in-the-groove: Down in the Groove was released in 1988, just before Dylan began the touring that would become known as the Never Ending Tour. It gathers covers and outtakes from several years of sessions, cut with very different casts, from Eric Clapton and Mark Knopfler to members of the Sex Pistols and the Clash. Two songs, "Silvio" and "Ugliest Girl in the World", were written with the Grateful Dead lyricist Robert Hunter, and members of the Dead sing on "Silvio", which became a regular in Dylan's concerts. The rest leans on rhythm and blues, country and folk, ending with a quiet reading of the Stanley Brothers' "Rank Strangers to Me". Because the tracks come from scattered sessions, the album has little shape, and critics treated it as a low point. Even so, his plain, worn singing on the folk and country songs points toward the traditional albums he would make a few years later.
albums.oh-mercy: Bono suggested that Dylan work with Daniel Lanois, and in early 1989 the two set up in a house in New Orleans that Lanois had turned into a studio. They worked mostly at night with a small group of local players, including Cyril Neville on percussion, and Lanois shaped a dark, humid sound of echoing guitars, low drums and close, intimate vocals. Dylan had arrived with new songs written over the previous year, and the album moves between social complaint, as in "Political World" and "Everything Is Broken", and private reckonings such as "Most of the Time" and "What Good Am I?". "Ring Them Bells" is played almost alone at the piano. The two men sometimes clashed, and songs such as "Dignity" and "Series of Dreams" were left off. Reviewers called it his best album in a decade, and Dylan's long account of the sessions in his memoir made it one of his most closely studied records.
albums.under-the-red-sky: Dylan made Under the Red Sky quickly in Los Angeles in early 1990 with the brothers Don and David Was producing, the same year he recorded with the Traveling Wilburys. A long list of famous players dropped in, among them George Harrison, Elton John, Slash, David Crosby, Bruce Hornsby and the brothers Stevie Ray and Jimmie Vaughan. The music is straightforward rock and blues, often built on short, simple riffs, and many of the songs are written like nursery rhymes or fables, with riddling characters and plain, repeating forms. The album is dedicated to a young child, which some listeners take as a key to its tone. Coming after Oh Mercy, it puzzled critics, and the opening "Wiggle Wiggle" was widely mocked. Over time more listeners have come to hear the fairy-tale songs, and the title track in particular, as deliberate and even haunting rather than careless.
albums.good-as-i-been-to-you: In 1992 Dylan began an album with a band and the guitarist David Bromberg, then set those sessions aside and recorded alone in his garage studio in Malibu. What came out was Good as I Been to You, thirteen old songs played on acoustic guitar and harmonica, with no originals at all. The material ranges across British and Irish ballads such as "Arthur McBride", American murder ballads and blues, and children's songs like "Froggie Went a Courtin'". His voice is hoarse and his guitar playing busy and inventive, giving the old songs a lived-in, unpolished feel very different from the folk revival recordings of thirty years earlier. Many listeners were surprised, but critics welcomed it as a return to his roots and a sign of renewed purpose. It began a period in which old songs fed his playing and writing, and it set up the darker companion album that followed a year later.
albums.world-gone-wrong: World Gone Wrong was recorded at home in Malibu in 1993, again with just Dylan's voice and acoustic guitar, and it went deeper into the old repertoire than its predecessor. Two songs come from the Mississippi Sheiks, one from Blind Willie McTell, and others from the long tradition of ballads about murder, war and wandering, ending with the hymn "Lone Pilgrim", which he learned from Doc Watson. The mood is heavier and the performances more stripped down, with his voice rough and close and his guitar loose and unhurried. Dylan also wrote his own liner notes, a sideways, playful essay on each song, tying it to its sources and to the troubles of the present. Critics praised its seriousness, and it won the Grammy for Best Traditional Folk Album. These two records reconnected him with the songs he had learned as a young man and prepared the ground for the original work that came later in the decade.
albums.time-out-of-mind: Dylan reunited with Daniel Lanois for Time Out of Mind, recording in Miami in early 1997 with a large band that included Jim Dickinson and Augie Meyers on keyboards, several guitarists and two drummers. The sessions were tense, as the two men again disagreed about sound, but the result is a murky, layered record in which Dylan's voice, now cracked and weathered, sits inside echoing guitars, organ and loose blues grooves. The songs keep returning to aging, lost love, distance and endurance, from the slow "Not Dark Yet" to the sixteen-minute closing ramble "Highlands". Shortly after the recording Dylan was hospitalized with a serious heart infection, and when the album came out that autumn many heard it through that news. Reviews were rapturous, and it won the Grammy for Album of the Year. "Make You Feel My Love" went on to be widely covered, and the record began the late period many count among his best.
albums.love-and-theft: Dylan recorded "Love and Theft" in New York in 2001 with his touring band of the time, including guitarists Larry Campbell and Charlie Sexton, bassist Tony Garnier and drummer David Kemper, along with Augie Meyers on keyboards. He produced it himself under the name Jack Frost, and the sessions were quick and relaxed. The music moves freely through older American styles: jump blues, rockabilly, swing, parlor ballads and crooner numbers, played with the ease of a band that knew him well. Dylan sings with wit and menace, and the songs are packed with borrowed lines and characters from old records, films and books, a habit that drew both admiration and debate. "Mississippi", left off Time Out of Mind, appears here in a warm new version. The album came out on the day of the September 11 attacks, yet critics embraced it, and it won the Grammy for Best Contemporary Folk Album.
albums.modern-times: Modern Times was recorded in New York early in 2006 with the band Dylan had been touring with, including Denny Freeman and Stu Kimball on guitars, Donnie Herron on steel guitar and violin, George Recile on drums and Tony Garnier on bass. Dylan again produced it as Jack Frost, and he spoke of wanting the record to capture how the band sounded live. The songs lean on older forms: Chicago-style blues shuffles, soft ballads built on prewar pop melodies, and long, slow numbers such as the closing "Ain't Talkin'". As on the record before it, he drew on older sources, and observers noticed lines echoing a Civil War-era poet, which renewed debate about borrowing. The album reached number one in America, his first in thirty years. It won a Grammy, and "Someday Baby" took another, for best solo rock vocal performance.
albums.christmas-in-the-heart: Christmas in the Heart came out in 2009, made with his touring musicians and guests including David Hidalgo of Los Lobos. It is a full holiday record of carols, pop standards and novelty songs, arranged in the warm style of the 1950s and early 1960s, with backing choirs, steel guitar and accordion. Dylan sings in his rough late voice, which made the earnest arrangements sound strange to some ears, and "Must Be Santa" became a rowdy polka with a comic video. Many wondered whether it was a joke. In interviews Dylan said plainly that it was not, and that he sang the songs as a believer and a fan of the music. Reaction ranged from delight to bafflement. All of his royalties went to hunger charities, including Feeding America in the United States, Crisis in Britain and the United Nations World Food Programme, which gave it an appeal beyond the music itself.
albums.together-through-life: Together Through Life began when the French director Olivier Dahan asked Dylan for a song for a film, and that one song grew into an album recorded quickly in late 2008. Dylan wrote almost all of it with Robert Hunter, the Grateful Dead lyricist he had worked with before. The sound comes from Chicago blues and the music of the Texas-Mexico border: shuffling rhythms, a low twanging guitar from Mike Campbell, and above all David Hidalgo's accordion, which colors nearly every song. The mood is relaxed and often playful, with love songs, road songs and wry complaints rather than the grand statements of his previous records, and his voice is at its most gravelly. One song borrows heavily from a Willie Dixon blues, and Dixon is credited. Reviewers generally liked it as a loose, easygoing side step, and it reached number one in both the US and the UK.
albums.tempest: Tempest was recorded in 2012 at Jackson Browne's studio in Santa Monica with Dylan's touring band and David Hidalgo, and Dylan again produced it as Jack Frost. It opens gently with "Duquesne Whistle", a jaunty swing number written with Robert Hunter, but much of what follows is dark: slow, grinding blues and long story-ballads in which betrayal and violence pile up. The title song runs about fourteen minutes and tells of the sinking of the Titanic in many verses over a lilting waltz, mixing historical figures with invented ones. The album closes with "Roll on John", a tribute to John Lennon built from echoes of Beatles songs. Dylan's voice is at its harshest here, and he uses it to growl and to tease. Critics praised its ambition and its storytelling, and it came out in the fiftieth anniversary year of his first album, which many reviews noted.
albums.shadows-in-the-night: For Shadows in the Night, Dylan took ten songs that Frank Sinatra had recorded and cut them at Capitol Studios in Hollywood, where Sinatra had made many of his records. Rather than copy the big orchestral arrangements, he scaled them down for his own five-piece band, with Donnie Herron's pedal steel carrying the lines once played by strings, and a few horns on some tracks. The musicians played together live around a small number of microphones, with engineer Al Schmitt capturing them with little or no overdubbing. The result is hushed and slow, and Dylan sings with surprising care and steadiness, staying close to the melodies. He said he saw the project not as covering Sinatra but as uncovering the songs. Many critics were moved by it, and he gave away copies to readers of a magazine for older Americans. It began the run of standards albums that filled the next three years.
albums.fallen-angels: Fallen Angels was recorded at Capitol Studios with the same small touring band and engineer Al Schmitt as Shadows in the Night, and it came out in 2016, shortly before Dylan turned seventy-five. Again the songs are ones Frank Sinatra had sung, but the choice is wider and the mood is lighter, with more swing and more songs of romance and longing alongside the ballads. The arrangements stay spare: steel guitar, soft electric guitars, upright bass and brushed drums, with an occasional horn. Dylan's singing is relaxed and assured, and he clearly enjoys phrasing these melodies. Reviewers found it warmer and more varied than its predecessor, though some wondered how long he would stay in this territory. It confirmed that the standards project was more than a one-off experiment, and later that year he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature, before returning to the same studio for a much larger set.
albums.triplicate: Triplicate came out in 2017, the year after Dylan was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature, and was his first three-disc album of new recordings. He recorded it at Capitol Studios in Hollywood with his touring band, this time with more horns in the arrangements, and arranged the thirty songs into three discs of ten, each given its own title and loosely following a mood. Some of the songs had been recorded by Frank Sinatra, while others reach wider across the American songbook, including "Stormy Weather" and "As Time Goes By". The playing is again gentle and unhurried, and Dylan's voice is patient and close, though the sheer length makes the record more of a long late-night program than a statement. Reviewers admired the care and craft but many felt the project had run its course. It was the last of his standards albums before he returned to writing his own songs.
albums.rough-and-rowdy-ways: Rough and Rowdy Ways arrived in June 2020, in the early months of the pandemic. Before it, Dylan released "Murder Most Foul", a long, slow meditation on the killing of John F. Kennedy and the American culture that followed it, which became his first song to top a Billboard chart. The album was made with his touring band and guests including the guitarist and producer Blake Mills. Its sound is quiet and spacious, moving between murmured ballads, heavy blues and slow, hymn-like pieces, with Dylan's voice close and calm. The songs range over history, myth, death, love and his own legend, packed with references to writers, musicians and films. "Key West (Philosopher Pirate)" drifts for nearly ten minutes, and "Murder Most Foul" fills a disc of its own. Critics greeted it as one of the great albums of his late career, and it showed he was still writing at full strength at seventy-nine.
